item.title: When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has gone from struggling with basic arithmetic to helping solve some of mathematics’ most famous open problems — and the field is reckoning with what that means.

Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University, describes the excitement and grief of watching A.I. take on work that gives people a sense of purpose — and asks what could be lost if machines deliver answers without the human struggle, insight and understanding that make solving problems meaningful.

Guest: Steven Strogatz, a professor of mathematics at Cornell University who writes for The New York Times about the future of research.

Background reading: 

  • Mathematics isn’t just a game to let A.I. solve — history shows why.
  • A.I. is mastering the kinds of projects that have long helped to build the careers of young mathematicians. What does that mean for their future?
  • Steven Strogatz’s forthcoming book: Big Math.

Photo: Ian C. Bates for The New York Times

item.title: The Israeli Film Directors Pushing for a Reckoning in Their Home Country
item.description:
The documentary film “NAZA,” which investigates the methods the Israeli military has used in the war in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, received a record-breaking standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival last month. Just a few days later, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would propose legislation that could revoke the directors’ Israeli citizenship, arguing that they had defamed their country.

Now, with a global theatrical release underway, the directors spoke with “The Daily” to discuss the film and all the pushback that it — and they — have experienced.

Guest: 

  • Rachel Szor, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and activist.
  • Yuval Abraham, an Israeli investigative journalist, film director and Arabic-Hebrew translator.

Background reading: 

  • After accolades abroad, “NAZA” met backlash at home.
  • Read The Times’s review of the film.

Photo: Stefano Rellandini/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, The Guardian/IFC Center, Ander Gillenea/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

item.title: Celine Dion’s Triumphant Return to the Stage
item.description:
A dramatic pop music comeback story is underway: Celine Dion is performing again.

In 2022, Dion, the renowned Canadian singer, announced that she had stiff person syndrome, a rare and incurable neurological disorder that causes painful muscle spasms and affects roughly one in a million people. The announcement came as a shock to her fans, and in a raw and revealing documentary released in 2024, “I Am: Celine Dion," she shared her struggle to overcome her condition, and sing again. But Dion worked her way back to performing, and is now appearing in a run of sold out shows in Paris.

The culture reporter Elisabeth Vincentelli was there on opening night, and in this episode of “The Sunday Daily,” she talks with our host Natalie Kitroeff about the remarkable comeback of Celine Dion.

On Today’s Episode:

  • Elisabeth Vincentelli, an arts, culture, and theater journalist.

Background Reading:

  • Celine Dion Is Back Onstage. Naturally, She Chose Paris.
  • Paris Really, Really Loves Celine Dion

Photo credit: Clementine Schneidermann for The New York Times.

item.title: She’s Been to Gaza. She Met With the Iranians. Now She Has a Warning.
item.description:
